Not that I'm supporting most of the argument that xcver is making, but

There are 10 R2's in the set:
Cracking the Wall
Dreams of the Sphinx

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Kushiel wrote:
> I'm gonna guess that R1 is more rare than R2. In that case, sure, I
> agree with this. It does seem like a separate issue from what xcver was
> making, though.

R2 means that the card shows up twice on the rare sheet, where the R1s
only show up once. For instance, assuming a sheet of cards has 100
cards on it, if there are 90 different rares, they are going to have 90
different cards on the sheet and the 10 of the rares are going to show
up twice (meaning 80 cards are R1 and 10 cards are R2). Then, as the
rare slot in a pack contains 1 card from the rare sheet pile, you have
twice the chance of ending up with any given R2 as you do an R1--with
perfect distribution which, in the grand scheeme, is always the case
(as there are a total of N rare sheets printed, and all of those cards
are in boosters somewhere, unless some of them got burned or ruined or
something), there are going to be, say, twice as many Telepathic Vote
Countings from 3rd in circulation as there are Hearts. And you'll get
twice as many. 'Cause in any given batch of 100 boosters, there should
be 1 Heart and 2 Telepathic Vote Countings.

So in any case, yeah, all the R2s very clearly should have been the new
cards, rather than the not new cards, as it wouldn't have made much of
a difference for the new players (as if they don't have any of the
rares, they are all new), but would have been great for the older
players (like, I don't need any more Telepathic Vote Countings, yet I
got far more Telepathic Vote Countings and Far Masteries which I also
don't need any more of than I did Iconnu Tutelage and Hearts...)

-Peter

I think the more general way to state this is, make the new cards
distinctly more common than you would in a normal set. For instance,
rares should be R2s - or even uncommons. Uncommons can be U2s or
commons. Commons can be C2s or C3s, whatever.

But I'm surprised we'd have to tell them. If you think about it,
that's precisely what they did in Legacies of Blood. And although
the 3-to-1 ratio may have been a bit severe for some of the in-demand
reprint rares, that might have been due to a number of complicating
issues: ratio of reprints to new cards, the large number of cards
printed in the overall set, reprints being unusually attractive
as "new layout" cards. In any event, it was clear that White
Wolf understood the basic principle. They just didn't apply it
Third Edition.

Fred

We conlfate ideas of rarity with what I'd like to call "relative
abundance". This is an issue similar to the "super-unobtainable rare
vampires from FN". IIRC from older calculations R1s from FN are 17
times less abundant than R2s.

Lets see what the math works out to be for new rares vs. reprint rares
in 3rd Ed;

A quick Monger search (Gawd bless Ethan Burrow!!!) tells us there are
12 new rares in the 3rd ed set. The WW 3rd Ed checklist page says there
are 90 rares sold in the boosters for this set.

(90-12)90*100 = 86.7% of the boosters you buy will contain reprint
rares. Said differently, out of every 30 boosters you buy, about 4 of
them will have a new rare. Said differently yet again, new rares are
6.5 times less abundant than reprint rares. Mediocre, but not _so_ bad,
especially as compared to FN R1's. The repartition issue will likely
skew reality away from this "ideal" estimate nastily (cf. Lasombra
getting one particluar rare only once in 15 boxes...) and contribute to
observed ebayistry.

DaveZ
Atom Weaver

As what others? Which other sets are you trying to compare 3rd Edition
to on a one-to-one basis, such that you could compare absolute number of
boosters purchased? Remember, 3E uses 100-card cardsheets for all rarity
levels (tempered slightly by the existance of a small number of R2s).
KMW used 50-card card cardsheets at all rarity levels (and had no
separate "uncommon" level). Legacies used two 50-card card sheets for
their 3-to-1 ratio of new cards to reprints - having the effect of being
a 66 2/3rd card cardsheet for new rares and a 200 card cardsheet for
reprint rares. (50 card cardsheet for vampires and the commons were, er,
rather complex.) Black Hand had some anomolies but was basically based on
50-card cardsheets. Gehenna was straight 50-card cardsheets. Anarchs
had some slight anomolies but was basically based on 50-card cardsheets.

You basically have to go back to Camarilla Edition to find another
set to find the same rarity levels - and Camarilla Edition has the
same problem this one does. And was printed for the same stated
purpose, leading one to conclude that Third Edition was likely based on
the Camarilla Edition model. The trouble is - when looked at that way -
that a number of Third Editions new library cards are much more useful
than Camarilla Edition's were. I think Baltimore Purge was about the
most useful new library card in that set.

> So all I've got is this anecdotal evidence, but it totally
> doesn't gel with what you're writing here.

Given the fact that there are more cards on the cardsheets, your
comparison doesn't tell you anything. I guess this is where set
size does matter.

And I rather believe in the practical application of my theory.
Certainly it's true in my case; I would have bought significantly more
boosters had the set contained all new cards at these rarity levels,
and happily so. As it is, I mostly sized my purchase based on the
number of new vampires I wanted to pick up and I've been kind of
throwing up my hands at the new library cards (or gritting my teeth
and overspending on EBAY for singles, where I've been able to stand
it). And the prices of new 3E singles on EBAY I've had to pay also
tends to confirm it. Not just HoN but all of them; HoN is just the
lightning rod discussion card, here. Mirror Walk is cool, for
instance. But it shouldn't be so cool that it's selling for over
$10 a card. Not for a common.

> And, as I wrote, there doesn't seem to be any way to get around what
> seems to be your issue with the rarity, aside from only ever printing
> sets with no reprints in the boosters. Yes/no?

Well, Peter's new/old idea is probably the way to go. Print new cards
at a relatively lower rarity level than they'd go for in an all-new
card set. This is, in effect, what they did with the 3-to-1 new to
reprint rare card ratio in Legacies. Perhaps the classic model for
it would be the 10th Anniversary Edition rares, where new cards were
essentially printed at twice the rarity level as the reprints, if you
bought one of each tin.

my subjective judgement that that HoN, particularly, is in high demand

Messages.Body:

news:1158965301.0...@d34g2000cwd.googlegroups.com...

>> I'm saying small numbers of new R1 cards in a set otherwise filled with
>> reprints are "super-rares" in effect. "Chase" is a word used to convey
>> my subjective judgement that that HoN, particularly, is in high demand
>> because it's such a great card.
>
> So how is this different from the new rares and uncommons from the
> Camarilla set, as you pointed out at the beginning of your post?

It isn't different. Except in that the Camarilla Edition new cards
weren't that useful on the whole. OK, Weighted Walking Stick - but
that was a common. It would have worked just fine as an uncommon
in an all-new-card set. Baltimore Purge would have worked just fine
as a rare. Tension in the Ranks was somewhat useful - but it was
printed as an R2. High Ground was a common. The others were so
strange I can't recall ever seeing them (though I'm probably forgetting
one or more).

The Third Edition cards seem to be - as a group - distinctly more
useful, IMHO. Otherwise, there's no difference between the two
sets.

> How would you fix this?

Ideally, I would put no new cards in a reprint set. White Wolf
doesn't seem to like their prospects of making sales under that
constraint, however. So I expect it's a non-starter of an idea.
Therefore, on to one that has a snowball's chance, which is...

Increase the commonality of new cards - DJ's idea (I guess). People
complained about reprints in LoB but LoB wasn't the same situation
in a number of ways. It wasn't printed to fulfill the same goal,
it was a combination of two different goals (reprint Bloodlines with
a few new Bloodlines cards plus print a set based on a new minor
sect). That caused other problems such as forcing people to buy
a set containing two themes even if they only wanted one of them.
(That is, I want Bloodlines reprints and I'm forced to accept
Laibon clan cards as well or vica versa.) Or the common cards such
as Tupdogs that weren't common enough. I think the complaints
voiced about reprints in Legacies were really just a catch-all
for all sorts of minor dissatisfactions that came up in LoB.
Bottom line, for 3E purposes, just making all the new cards less
rare would go a long way in fixing the problem without much of
a drawback.

And not printing undercosted cards wouldn't hurt.

Fred

Oops. Yeah, it is the main reason why.
But of course the contents of the set have some weight in this too. I'd
say the only reason why it's not as big a factor when compared to the
priting errors is that very few people actually have that many copies
of some reprints, except for most commons, since very few people were
actually able to buy multiple boxes when Sabbat War came out. So in
here, the fact that the set is geared mostly for new players doesn't
matter *that* much - as long as the distribution is good, that old
player can live with +X more copies of that uncommon he already has if
he gets +X copies of, say, Weighted Walking Stick or Freak Drive or
whatever along.

I'd risk saying that people wouldn't bother about the printing errors
here if the distribution was acceptable. Too few players are actually
collectors and most are only interested in playing value. But going
through all the effort to import boxes to end up with no [Rare X] or no
[Uncommon Y] is too much. Up to this weekend, some of us had read the
reports in this newsgroup and got worried, but seeing the actual result
of 3 opened boxes cristalized that general stance in most players'
minds. In the end, the wacky distribution can make an older player feel
like he got very few things of interest, just like if he had bought too
many of Sabbat War before. Actually, it's even worse, since he was
expecting to find use for some reprints and didn't got even that.

Not that it matters in the grand scheme of things, just imparting some
of the general feel in here.

Fabio "Sooner222" Macedo

It's more or less my point too. The distribution in itself causes some
sort of artificial rarity. Of course if you're totally new to this and
only had 3rd Edition it wouldn't been any rarer than for example black
forest base (has anyone got one to spare?) but in a larger context of
sets and adding that a lot of decks might want to use this card (even as
a 1 of) the demand is high. Take Week of Nightmares which was in Final
Nights and thus also very "rare". This only goes in decks of one clan as
a one or two-of. Considering it's worth one can understand why Heart is
valued this high atm. Putting the new cards in the R2 slot would've been
a good opportunity to lessen the impact somewhat but they didn't (only 2
rather crappy ones) so market has to live with the demand in comparison
to it's supply until there comes a precon to fix it (as we know certain
card insertions into precon's was meant to deflate card prices
somewhat...back before it was in a starter DotS was hard to get too and
don't get me started on Tomb of Rameses III before it was errata'd).
